family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Start with a woody plant bearing alternate simple leaves and tiny axillary flowers. Then ask whether the plant is deciduous or evergreen, compare leaf texture/margins, and confirm a superior ovary developing into a fleshy drupe with several hard pyrenes.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Alternate simple leaves + tiny mostly 4–5-merous unisexual flowers on dioecious plants + superior ovary + berry-like drupe containing several pyrenes.
core_characters: Trees or shrubs; local learner taxa are woody.
Leaves simple and alternate; texture ranges from thin/deciduous to thick/coriaceous evergreen.
Margins may be crenate, serrate, entire, or spinose depending on species.
Stipules are minute and easy to miss; do not teach their absence as absolute.
Flowers are small, actinomorphic, usually 4–5-merous and axillary.
Staminate flowers have functional stamens plus a reduced pistillode.
Pistillate flowers have a superior multi-loculed ovary plus staminodes.
The style is very short or absent and the broad/discoid stigma often persists on the fruit.
Fruit is a drupe, not a true botanical berry, and typically contains several hard 1-seeded pyrenes.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not identify hollies by red fruit alone; all three project Ilex can show red drupes.
Do not teach holly leaves as always spiny; yaupon and possumhaw are not strongly spine-toothed.
Do not teach the family as always evergreen; Ilex decidua is a major local deciduous exception.
Do not call the fruits true berries in the botanical lesson; they are drupes with multiple pyrenes.
Do not infer Central Texas nativity from nursery/landscape occurrence, especially Ilex opaca.

local_key: Deciduous + larger thin crenate leaves + red/orange drupes on bare winter twigs -> Ilex decidua.
Evergreen + tiny leathery leaves with low rounded crenate teeth + multi-stem shrub/small tree -> Ilex vomitoria.
Evergreen tree + much larger thick leaves with stiff spine-tipped teeth -> Ilex opaca comparison; strict target-zone FAIL.

anchor_cards.look_here_first: Possumhaw becomes easiest in winter: the leaves drop, leaving red/orange drupes packed along pale gray twigs. In leaf, the blades are larger and thinner than yaupon and shallowly crenate to crenate-serrate.
confirms: Shallow crenate to crenate-serrate margin; not stiffly spiny.
Tiny axillary unisexual flowers; plants primarily dioecious.
Red to orange-red drupes persisting after leaf drop.

sex_comparison.lesson: This family is ideal for teaching dioecy visually.
sex_comparison.staminate_male: Flowers show conspicuous functional stamens/anthers around a reduced central pistillode; these plants do not set normal drupes.
sex_comparison.pistillate_female: Flowers show a broad superior ovary with a conspicuous sessile/discoid stigma and reduced staminodes; these are the plants that later bear drupes.

fruit_lesson.key_point: The red 'berry' is botanically a drupe with multiple hard pyrenes.

Ebenaceae.confusion: Alternate simple leaves, unisexual flowers and fleshy fruit can overlap.
Ebenaceae.tie_breaker: Diospyros fruit carries a very conspicuous enlarged persistent calyx and generally larger seeds; Ilex has small axillary flowers and a small drupe with several pyrenes and often a persistent discoid stigma.

Sapotaceae.confusion: Woody evergreen plants with alternate leaves and fleshy fruit can overlap.
Sapotaceae.tie_breaker: Sapotaceae commonly has milky latex and fruit with a few large glossy seeds; Ilex lacks the milky-latex cue and has several hard pyrenes.

Rhamnaceae.confusion: Woody plants with small flowers and drupaceous fruit can overlap.
Rhamnaceae.tie_breaker: Rhamnaceae often has evident stipules and characteristic arcuate/strong basal venation; Ilex has tiny axillary unisexual flowers, dioecy, and several pyrenes.
